title: A shell command assembled from a value the caller chooses
control:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.exec('ls ' + req.query.dir); }

peers.contract: detects instances of child_process & non-literal exec()

cases.label: request value concatenated into exec
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.exec('ls ' + req.query.dir); }
cases.why: A shell metacharacter in the query string runs a second command.

cases.label: the same via a template literal
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.exec(`ls ${req.query.dir}`); }

cases.label: ESM import spelling
cases.code:
import cp from 'node:child_process';
function f(req) { cp.exec('ls ' + req.body.dir); }
cases.why: The module spelling does not change the defect.

cases.label: destructured exec
cases.code:
const { exec } = require('child_process');
function f(req) { exec('ls ' + req.query.dir); }
cases.why: Destructuring hides the receiver, not the sink.

cases.label: a fully literal command
cases.why: The command is written in the file.

cases.label: execFile with a caller-chosen argument
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.execFile('ls', [req.query.dir]); }
cases.why: Written as a decoy on the assumption that no shell means no defect. Executed: `execFileSync('echo', ['safe; echo PWNED'])` yields the literal string, so command injection is indeed impossible — but the caller still chooses an ARGUMENT, and a leading `-` is a flag. The rule reports CWE-88 argument injection here, not CWE-78, and goes silent once `--` terminates option parsing. The rule was right and the case was wrong.

cases.label: spawn with a caller-chosen argument
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.spawn('ls', [req.query.dir]); }
cases.why: Written as a decoy on the assumption that no shell means no defect. Executed: `execFileSync('echo', ['safe; echo PWNED'])` yields the literal string, so command injection is indeed impossible — but the caller still chooses an ARGUMENT, and a leading `-` is a flag. The rule reports CWE-88 argument injection here, not CWE-78, and goes silent once `--` terminates option parsing. The rule was right and the case was wrong.

cases.label: a call to something else named exec
the documented fix
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.execFile('ls', ['--', req.query.dir]); }
cases.why: Reporting the fix leaves the user nothing to do.

knownLimits: `execFile`/`spawn` with a caller-chosen argument report CWE-88 (argument injection), not CWE-78. eslint-plugin-security does not model argument injection at all, so it is silent on both — which reads as better precision and is less coverage.
`execFile('ls', ['--', x])` is silent: `--` terminates option parsing, so the value can no longer be read as a flag.
